sections.title: Vowel length: a / aa
sections.explain:
German has long and short vowels, and the length changes the meaning: Staat (state) is not Stadt (city). French has no such contrast, so French speakers tend to give every vowel the same medium length, and Germans hear the wrong word.

Spelling tells you the length:

  • Long: double vowel (Staat), vowel + h (Bahn), one consonant after the vowel (Tag, Name).
  • Short: double consonant (Stadt has dt, Kamm has mm) or two or more consonants (Apfel, Mann).

For a, the quality barely changes: only the duration does. So timing is everything.
sections.howto:
1. Open your mouth as for the French a in papa, tongue low and flat.
  2. Long a: hold the vowel for about two beats, like a relaxed sigh aaah, then close softly: BA:N.
  3. Short a: one quick beat, then cut it off hard with the next consonant, as if the consonant arrives early: BANN.
  4. Practise by tapping: two taps for long a, one tap for short a.

pairs.heardAforB: You said Stadt but it sounded like Staat: your a was too long. Make it short and crisp, like the a in French 'patte', and snap straight into the next consonant.

sections.title: Vowel length: e / ee / eh
sections.explain:
With e, length and quality change together. Long e is a closed, tense é held long (Beet, Weg). Short e is an open è, cut short (Bett, weg). The letter ä sounds like short e when short (fällen).

French has both é and è, which helps, but French never holds a vowel long, so wen and wenn can sound the same.

Spelling: ee, eh or e + one consonant = long (Beet, fehlen, den). Double consonant or a consonant cluster = short (Bett, denn, stellen). Weg (way) is long but weg (away) is short: learn that one by heart.
sections.howto:
1. Long e: smile slightly, tongue high and tense, say French é and hold it for two beats: BÉ:T.
  2. Short e: relax the jaw a little lower, say French è and stop it after one beat: BÈTT.
  3. Do not glide: German long e stays pure, no é-i like in English day.

pairs.heardAforB: You said Bett but it sounded like Beet: your e was too long. Make it an open, short 'è' as in French 'mettre', and snap straight into the next consonant.

sections.title: Vowel length: i / ie
sections.explain:
Long i (ie, ih, sometimes i + one consonant) is a tense French i held long: Miete. Short i (before a double consonant or a cluster) is shorter and more open, almost between French i and é: Mitte.

French speakers usually say every i as a short tense French i. That makes Miete too short and Mitte too tense, and the two words merge.

Spelling rule: ie is always long (Lied, Bier, vier). ih is long (ihn, ihr). i before tt, ss, ll, ff, nn or two consonants is short (Mitte, Schiff, Kind).
sections.howto:
1. Long i: wide smile, tongue high and tense, hold for two beats: MI:-te.
  2. Short i: relax the lips and let the tongue drop a tiny bit, one beat only: MIT-te.
  3. Think of short i as the vowel in English sit, not French si.

sections.title: Vowel length: o / oo / oh
sections.explain:
Long o is closed and rounded, like French ô in eau or côte, but held longer: Ofen. Short o is open, like French o in porte, and short: offen.

French has both qualities, so the main job is timing. French speakers often shorten the long o, so Ofen drifts towards offen.

Spelling: oo, oh or o + one consonant = long (Boot, Sohn, Ton, Brot). o before a double consonant or a cluster = short (offen, Sonne, Post).
sections.howto:
1. Long o: round the lips into a small circle, as for French eau, and hold two beats: O:-fen.
  2. Short o: open the jaw a little more, lips less rounded, as in porte, one beat: OF-fen.
  3. Keep long o pure: no glide to ou at the end.

sections.title: Vowel length: u / uh
sections.explain:
German u is always French ou, never French u. Long u is a tense ou held long: Mus, Mut, Fuß. Short u is shorter and a little more open, between ou and o: muss, Mutter.

French speakers usually make every u the same, and the very common muss then sounds like Mus (purée).

Spelling: uh, u + ß or u + one consonant = long (Ruhm, Fuß, gut). u before ss, tt, nn, ck or a cluster = short (muss, Mutter, Hund).
sections.howto:
1. Long u: push the lips forward into a tight circle, tongue back, hold two beats: MOU:T.
  2. Short u: lips less tight, jaw a bit lower, one beat: MOUSS.
  3. Never read German u as French u (that is German ü).

pairs.note: One s = long, ss = short. muss is a top A1 word.
pairs.heardBforA: You said Mus but it sounded like muss: your u was too short. Hold it about twice as long, a French 'ou' held for two beats with tightly rounded lips, and keep it tense.
pairs.heardAforB: You said muss but it sounded like Mus: your u was too long. Make it a short, relaxed 'ou', almost towards French 'o', and snap straight into the next consonant.

sections.title: Vowel length: ü, ö, ä
sections.explain:
Good news: French already has the umlaut sounds. German ü = French u (tu), long ö = French eu in deux, short ö = French eu in peur.

The challenge is again length. Long ü and ö are tense and held (Hüte, Höhle). Short ü and ö are quick and a bit more relaxed (Hütte, Hölle).

Spelling works as for the other vowels: üh/öh or one consonant = long; double consonant or cluster = short. ä is long è in wählen, short è in Hände or Äpfel.
sections.howto:
1. Long ü: say French tu, then hold the vowel two beats: HU:-te.
  2. Short ü: same lips, slightly looser, one beat: HUT-te.
  3. Long ö: French deux, held: HEU:-le. Short ö: French peur, one beat: HEUL-le.

pairs.note: Long closed ö (deux) vs short open ö (peur).
pairs.heardBforA: You said Höhle but it sounded like Hölle: your ö was too short. Hold it for two beats with tense, rounded lips.
pairs.heardAforB: You said Hölle but it sounded like Höhle: your ö was too long. Keep it short and slightly relaxed, then go straight into the consonant.

pairs.heardAforB: You said Hütte but it sounded like Hüte: your ü was too long. Keep it short and slightly relaxed, then go straight into the consonant.

sections.title: Word stress
sections.explain:
French puts a light accent on the last syllable of a word group. German stresses one syllable per word strongly (louder, longer, higher), and the others are reduced.

  • Native German words: stress on the first syllable (ARbeit, MORgen, AUFstehen, BAHNhof).
  • Prefixes be-, ver-, ge-, er-, ent-, zer- are never stressed: the stress goes to the stem (verSTEhen, beZAHlen).
  • Loanwords, often French ones, stress late (MuSIK, ToiLETte, UniversiTÄT). Verbs in -ieren stress -IE- (studIEren).

A few words change meaning with stress (UMfahren knock over vs umFAHren drive around).
sections.howto:
1. Find the stressed syllable (capitals in the approximation).
  2. Make it louder and longer, and raise the pitch slightly.
  3. Reduce the other syllables, especially e in -en, -e, -el: almost swallow them.
  4. Clap once on the stressed syllable while you speak.

sections.title: The ich-Laut [ç]
sections.explain:
The ich-Laut [ç] is the sound in ich, nicht, Milch. French has no such sound, so French speakers replace it with ch as in chat and say isch. To a German ear that is sch, so Kirche (church) becomes Kirsche (cherry), and mich becomes misch.

[ç] is a whispered French y (as in yeux): air hissing between the middle of the tongue and the hard palate, lips not rounded.

Where: after e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu, after l, n, r, in -chen and in the ending -ig (richtig, zwanzig). In Switzerland, -ig is often said with a k (zwanzik); for the exam either is fine.

1. Say French yeux slowly and freeze on the y.
  2. Now whisper it: no voice, just air. That hiss is [ç].
  3. Keep a slight smile; do not round or push the lips forward (that would make sch).
  4. Practise i + hiss: i... ç, then ich, mich, dich, nicht.

sections.title: ich-Laut vs ach-Laut
sections.explain:
German ch has two sounds, and the vowel before it decides which one:

  • ach-Laut [x] after a, o, u, au: a throaty friction at the back, like Spanish jota (Bach, Buch, Nacht, auch). French speakers usually find this easy: it is close to a voiceless French r.
  • ich-Laut [ç] everywhere else: after e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu, after consonants, and always in -chen (Bäche, Bücher, Nächte, euch, Mädchen).

Plurals with umlaut switch the sound: Buch [x] becomes Bücher [ç]. The tongue simply follows the vowel.
sections.howto:
1. ach-Laut: after a back vowel, raise the back of the tongue towards the soft palate and push air: BAKH.
  2. ich-Laut: after a front vowel, the hiss moves forward to the hard palate, lips in a smile: BÈ-ch'e.
  3. Say the pairs in a row (Buch, Bücher) and feel the friction slide from the back to the front of the mouth.

sections.title: Aspirated p, t, k
sections.explain:
At the start of a stressed syllable, German p, t, k are aspirated: a little puff of air follows them, like a whispered h: Tee = tʰÉ:. French p, t, k have no puff.

The problem: German b, d, g are often only weakly voiced. So German ears tell p from b mainly by the puff, not by voicing. A French unaspirated p therefore sounds like a German b: Pass becomes Bass, Tank becomes Dank, Karten becomes Garten.

No puff after s/sch (Sport, Stadt) and less in unstressed syllables.

sections.title: Final devoicing (Auslautverhärtung)
sections.explain:
At the end of a word or syllable, German b, d, g are pronounced p, t, k: Tag = TA:K, Hund = HOUNT, gelb = GUÈLP. French keeps them voiced (bague, grande), so French speakers say a soft d or g, often with a little e muet after it.

When an ending is added, the consonant moves into the next syllable and becomes voiced again: Tag (k) but Tage (g), Hund (t) but Hunde (d).

So some words are perfect homophones: Rad = Rat, seid = seit. Note: the recognizer usually still understands a voiced final, so listen to the model and copy the hard ending.

1. At the end of a word, read b, d, g as p, t, k: no vibration in the throat (touch your throat to check).
  2. Stop cleanly: no little vowel after the consonant (not Tague, just TA:K).
  3. When an ending follows (Tage, Hunde), switch back to a soft, voiced b, d, g.

sections.title: Vocalized r and the -er ending
sections.explain:
After a vowel, German r is usually not a consonant at all: it becomes a light a-like vowel. vier = FI:A, Uhr = OU:A, hier = HI:A.

The ending -er becomes a short, open a [ɐ]: Lehrer = LÉ:-ra, Mutter = MOUT-ta. French speakers tend to read it as -ère with a full r (Lehrère), or as an e muet, which turns bitter into bitte.

The ending -e stays a weak e muet. So -e vs -er is a real contrast: Miete (rent) vs Mieter (tenant).
sections.howto:
1. For -e: barely say a French e as in le, jaw almost closed.
  2. For -er: drop the jaw a little and say a short, light a, without any r friction.
  3. For r after a long vowel (vier, Uhr): hold the vowel, then glide into a soft a.
  4. Before a vowel (Lehrer: the first r), keep your normal French r.

sections.title: The German h
sections.explain:
In French, h is never pronounced. In German, h at the start of a word or syllable is always breathed out, like fogging up a mirror: Haus, Hund, hier. Without it, Haus becomes aus and Hund becomes und.

Some French speakers then overcorrect and add h to words starting with a vowel (Hende for Ende).

Important: h after a vowel is silent. It only shows that the vowel is long: sehr = ZÉ:A, gehen = GUÉ:-en, Uhr = OU:A, fahren = FA:-ren.
sections.howto:
1. Open your mouth for the vowel, then breathe out through it before the vowel starts: h-aus.
  2. The h is pure breath: no friction in the throat (not the ach-Laut, not a French r).
  3. For words with a vowel start (aus, und, Ende), begin the vowel crisply with no breath.
  4. Inside words after a vowel (gehen, sehr), ignore the h and lengthen the vowel.

sections.title: ü and ö vs i, u, o, e
sections.explain:
This is your French advantage: German ü is French u (tu), German ö is French eu (deux, peur). English and Spanish speakers struggle here; you do not.

But there are two traps:

  • Spelling trap: German u is French ou. If you read Mutter the French way, you say Mütter (mothers).
  • Plurals: many plurals add an umlaut (Bruder, Brüder; Tochter, Töchter). Make the umlaut clearly audible, or the plural disappears.

Also keep i (spread lips) and ü (rounded lips) apart: vier vs für.
sections.howto:
1. German u = French ou. German ü = French u. Never mix them.
  2. German long o = French ô (eau), short o = o of porte. German ö = French eu (long: deux, short: peur).
  3. i vs ü: same tongue position; only the lips change, spread for i, rounded for ü.

sections.title: Uvular r (your French advantage)
sections.explain:
Good news: the standard German r at the start of a word or syllable, or after a consonant, is the same uvular r as in French: rot, Reis, Brot, drei. You can use your normal French r here.

In Zürich you will also hear a rolled, tongue-tip r. Both are correct; for the exam, your French r is perfect.

Only after a vowel does the German r soften into a light a (vier, Uhr, Lehrer): see the section on vocalized r.
sections.howto:
1. Use your French r before vowels and after consonants: Brot, Frau, grün.
  2. Keep it light: a soft friction, not a strong scrape.
  3. Do not drop it in clusters: Straße = CHTRA:-sse, with a clear r.

pairs.note: Only r vs l.

sections.title: Shadowing: everything together
sections.explain:
Shadowing means repeating a sentence right after the model voice, copying its rhythm, melody and sounds as exactly as you can. It trains everything at once: vowel length, stress, ich-Laut, aspiration, final devoicing, -er and h.

Each sentence below lists its main traps. Listen first, then speak along with the voice, then alone into the microphone.

Do short sessions every day: five sentences, five minutes. Regular short practice fixes rhythm faster than one long session per week.
sections.howto:
1. Listen to the sentence twice without speaking.
  2. Read the focus line and find the traps in the sentence.
  3. Speak together with the voice, at the same speed.
  4. Record yourself alone and compare. Repeat until the recognizer gets every word.
